transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-18
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52m
Attendees: Maria Chen (Redwood AE), Jonah Patel (Redwood SE), Asha Rao (LumenEdge CTO), Daniel Kim (ML Eng), Priya Singh (Infra)

Auto-summary: quick review of caching experiments, batching tradeoffs, next steps to validate tokens/sec/$ over 24h window.

[00:00] Maria (Redwood): hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — recap the experiments from last week and walk through cost/unit numbers. Jonah will run the deeper benchmark.
[00:28] Asha (LumenEdge): yep thanks. we've been seeing spikes in tokens/sec during business hours and then cold starts in the evening which blow the unit economics. hoping caching helps.
[01:03] Jonah (Redwood): short recap — we ran three config sets: baseline (no caching, baseline batch=1), prefix caching enabled (KV warm up persisted across requests), and aggressive batching (batch size up to 8, dynamic batching windows). numbers are in the sheet Maria shared but top-line: prefix caching improved tokens/sec/$ by roughly 1.9x on the chat flow when warm, and aggressive batching cut raw compute cost ~30% but added about ~6–8% p99 latency.
[01:45] Daniel (LumenEdge): interesting. when you say warm, what's the hit rate we should expect? our traffic has a long tail of infrequent prompts.
[02:10] Jonah: good q. in our run the cache hit rate after a 2-hour steady-state reached 68% on the scripted prompt set; with the real traffic distribution we think hit rate could be lower, maybe 45–60% depending on prompt similarity. prefix caching benefits more on repeated system prompts and multi-turn sessions.
[02:44] Priya: so that 1.9x tokens/sec/$ is optimistic for our real-world mix?
[02:58] Maria: yeah that's why we want a 24-hour benchmark using your actual prompt distribution. the earlier run used synthetic workload that favored repeated prefixes.
[03:15] Asha: okay makes sense. can you walk through latency tradeoffs with batching? we need sub-150ms p50 for core searches.
[03:40] Jonah: sure — baseline had median ~45ms locally and p99 ~230ms on the host. aggressive batching pushed cost down, median stayed ~55ms but p99 increased to ~250–260ms. there's room to tune the batching window: smaller windows give most of the cost benefit with less p99 impact. we recommended a sweet spot around batch=4 and dynamic timeout 8–12ms which cut cost ~22% and kept p99 under 200ms in our env. caveat: results vary by hw and sequence length.
[04:22] Daniel: quick follow-up — what about KV cache eviction and memory pressure? we run moderate seq lengths (avg 600 tokens) so KV size is non-trivial.
[04:40] Jonah: good point. our runtime supports per-shard kv eviction policies; for your sequence lengths we suggested a sliding window TTL of ~20 minutes and a max-kv bytes cap per session. this keeps memory within the dedicated pool targets. on hosted we can configure similar limits but you'll get more predictable performance on Dedicated.
[05:05] Asha: Dedicated still sounds expensive — how are you modeling tokens/sec/$ vs the reserved capacity premium?
[05:20] Maria: in short, Dedicated reduces per-token variability and improves tail latency, but you pay a reserved capacity premium. our cost model compares hosted spot-like pricing vs dedicated amortized cost: for high steady throughput (>50M tokens/day) Dedicated often wins on $/token and SLOs, otherwise hosted with caching & batching might be best. we'll share the spreadsheet with break-even points for your daily volume.
[05:55] Priya: security question — if we go Private (VPC) how does key management and audit logging look? we need KMS integration and retention logs for 12 months.
[06:14] Maria: Redwood Private supports bringing your KMS (AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure) plus HSM integrations in enterprise plans; audit logs can be exported to your S3/BigQuery for 12+ months. we'll include the compliance checklist in the security doc pack.
[06:35] Daniel: on model variants — we tried a 4-bit quantized variant; accuracy seemed okay on generative tests but we need to run your eval harness on our prompts. any guidance?
[06:52] Jonah: quantization reduces memory and cost but can shift token distributions. we recommend running a small A/B: quantized vs fp16 on a 1,000 prompt sample and measure exact-match and perplexity; our Optimize toolkit will highlight regression thresholds. for many chat workloads 4-bit is fine but content-risk prompts can suffer.
[07:20] Asha: okay. can you summarize the recommended immediate config for us to test?
[07:30] Jonah: yes — three profiles: 1) conservative: prefix caching enabled, batch=2, dynamic timeout 6ms; 2) balanced: prefix caching, batch=4, timeout 10ms; 3) aggressive: prefix caching + larger micro-batch up to 8, timeout 15ms and larger cache TTL. Run each for a sustained 24-hour window to capture diurnal effects.
[07:58] Maria: and we'll compute tokens/sec/$ for warm vs cold windows and give you a delta table.
[08:10] Daniel: what about warm-up strategies? can we pre-warm KV or schedule background prefetches to improve morning tail?
[08:26] Jonah: absolutely — pre-warming common sessions and priming KV for known user cohorts helps. we also support scheduled micro-batches during low-usage windows to keep kv warmed without user impact. cost to pre-warm is small compared to saving repeated cold-starts.
[08:45] Asha: any gotchas with customer data? we have PII in prompts.
[08:52] Maria: we recommend redaction pipeline and token-level masking for PII, plus selecting Private or Dedicated if you need full network isolation. also we support payload encryption at rest/in-flight. we'll include the redaction best-practices doc.
[09:10] Daniel: last week you reported a caching bug that dropped hit rate for long sessions — was that addressed?
[09:19] Jonah: yes that was a mis-serialization of the KV keys on multi-turn threads; fixes are deployed on the staging runtime and in production rollout next week — shouldn't affect your planned runs.
[09:32] Priya: good. on the benchmark, do you need any infra access or keys?
[09:39] Maria: for hosted runs no infra changes needed; for Private we'd need a staging VPC peering or agent. but for now the 24-hour run will use your sample prompts against our hosted cluster; we'll anonymize logs.
[09:55] Asha: sounds good. timeline?
[10:00] Maria: I'll share the spreadsheet today (action). Jonah will kick off the 24-hour benchmark by next Wednesday and deliver results within 3 business days after the run.
[10:12] Daniel: any preliminary numbers you can share now for the batch=4 balanced profile?
[10:18] Jonah: from our synthetic run: balanced profile gave ~22% cost reduction vs baseline, tokens/sec/$ improved ~1.6x in warm windows, p99 stayed ~10–12% higher than baseline but within reasonable ranges.
[10:35] Asha: okay we'll supply the prompt set by Friday.
[10:40] Maria: great — also quick note on fallback policies: we recommend a two-tier fallback — model-size fallback first (smaller quantized variant) then region fallback. keeps user experience smoother than blackouts.
[10:55] Priya: ok can Redwood produce recommended rollback thresholds for quality so our app can auto-fallback?
[11:03] Jonah: yes we can provide webhook triggers tied to eval set metrics; we'll share suggested thresholds in the spreadsheet.
[11:18] Asha: final — do you have a rough estimate on cost delta if we enable 4-bit quant + balanced batching vs hosted baseline?
[11:29] Jonah: back-of-envelope: quantization gives another ~15–25% compute saving; combined with balanced batching you're in the 35–45% total compute cost reduction range assuming decent cache hit rates. will confirm with the concrete numbers post-benchmark.
[11:45] Maria: ok let's recap next steps — Jonah run extended runs; I share cost model; LumenEdge sends prompt set and security contact. schedule follow-up after results.
[12:00] Asha: thanks all, this was helpful.

End of transcript.

Recap / next meeting plan: tentatively week of 2027-01-08 for results review.
